Stated Claim / Post Context:
Nepalese Australian delivers blunt warning on the ABC over 'huge' migrant numbers: 'It stresses everything'

A Nepalese Australian has warned that rapid population growth is making it harder for new arrivals to understand the country's identity.

Actual Article Body:
By BURNEY WONG - NEWS REPORTER

Published:  08:56 AEDT, 28 October 2026   |  Updated:  09:05 AEDT, 28 October 2026

A Nepalese Australian has warned that soaring immigration could dilute the country’s identity and leave new arrivals with no clear sense of what it means to be Australian.

Net permanent and long-term arrivals totalled 494,540 in the 12 months to January 2026, a near-record figure, according to Australian Bureau of Statistics data.

The net figure for January alone was 57,270, the highest recorded for that month.

Shankar, who was identified only by his first name, appeared on ABC National Forum last month as an audience member and argued that rapid population growth was making it harder for newcomers to understand what it meant to be Australian.

'When people come in, they need to have a reference point,' he told host David Speers.

'The majority of the panel members that are sitting over there, they had a reference point to what Australia was: an identity.

'And I understand that that identity has been changing over time, but when you start to increase the population in a very short period of time, you start to dilute what that identity is.'

Pointing to Western Sydney as an example, Shankar questioned what shared cultural reference point was available to new migrants settling in the region.

Shankar, a Nepalese Australian, has warned that soaring immigration could dilute the country’s identity and leave new arrivals with no clear sense of what it means to be Australian

'What do they assimilate to, what do they aspire to?... You can't just say it's multiculturalism, because if you try to cater to everybody, you become nothing,' he said.

Speers then asked what migrants were doing that worried him.

'Migrants aren't doing anything per se, but what we're seeing is certain types of religious groups that are advocating for their needs and wants and getting to the high level of politics to advocate for that... You bring in a certain group in huge numbers and it stresses everything,' Shankar replied.

Shankar described Australia’s identity as a mixture of Indigenous foundations and ‘Anglo-Saxon heritage, which is all around us and institutions are based on that’.

'The reason that this country is so well thought about, is that people can come in and look at that identity and forge something for themselves,' he said.

However, when Speers asked whether the Anglo-Saxon identity he mentioned should be preserved, Shankar argued that culture should instead evolve.

'You don't preserve a culture, like in a museum,' he said.

'What you do, is you take the good bits and you build upon it.'

Shankar told host David Speers (pictured): ‘When people come in, they need to have a reference point’

Shankar also argued that rapid population growth was ‘fracturing’ Australia’s shared identity.

'What's happening at the moment is that it is being fractured, because you've got many different groups coming in large numbers saying, "Actually, we don't like that",' he said.

'That might be something that's taken 100 years to progress, so we're getting a bit of a challenge.'

When Speers asked how his own experiences reflected his views, Shankar said: ‘The government has allowed for this; it’s not the migrants themselves.’

The debate comes as the Albanese government has kept the 2026–27 Permanent Migration Program at 185,000 places, unchanged from 2025–26, although allocations within the program have shifted.

The Coalition has pledged to cut net overseas migration to 100,000 for its first two years in government, before increasing it to 130,000 in the third year and 160,000 in the fourth.

It says its policies would reduce Australia’s temporary migrant population by about 650,000 over four years.

One Nation has proposed cutting 750,000 temporary visas, which it says would drive net overseas migration below zero for three years before it rose to 130,000 in the fourth year.
